evidence.title: Mission termination after RCS activation
evidence.body: Both rings of the reentry control system have been activated to regain control, and substantial propellant has been used. Under these conditions, mission rules require termination. Cancel the remaining objectives and prepare a contingency return.

provenance.note: Automatic at briefing; reference. Historical termination principle H2; game selection boundary F7.

evidence.title: Network coverage and report timing
evidence.body: The last report tells us what was true when the crew sent it. Between tracking passes, we have no new information about their condition. Keep the report's observation time beside it; mark anything since that time as unconfirmed. The crew must act on their own until the next station acquires their signal.

provenance.note: Automatic at briefing; instructional reference grounded in H1.

evidence.title: Contact drill: instruction and readback
evidence.body: Houston CAPCOM sends the instruction to the tracking-ship CAPCOM, who reads it back and confirms receipt. FLIGHT checks the confirmation before treating the instruction as received. Mark missing observation times as unknown.

provenance.note: Acquired by g8-prep-contact; original F1 reference. Named practice calls and desk roles are original game exercises, not a claim that these exact rehearsals occurred before Gemini VIII.

evidence.title: Recovery drill: pickup instruction
evidence.body: Elias passes the aircraft's location report to the DoD recovery coordinator. They identify the desk that will send the ship its pickup instruction and check the readback. Record aircraft support and the ship's arrival separately.

provenance.note: Acquired by g8-prep-recovery; original F2 reference. Named practice calls and desk roles are original game exercises, not a claim that these exact rehearsals occurred before Gemini VIII.

evidence.title: Systems drill: low-propellant warning
evidence.body: Mara reports the RCS propellant warning to FLIGHT and CAPCOM together. She states what the instruments show, what remains uncertain, and the response she recommends for entry. CAPCOM reads the recommendation back before passing it on.

provenance.note: Acquired by g8-prep-systems; original F3 reference. Named practice calls and desk roles are original game exercises, not a claim that these exact rehearsals occurred before Gemini VIII.

evidence.title: Docking confirmed.
evidence.body: The crew have confirmed docking with Agena.

provenance.note: Docking event; H3. No roll data appended during gap.

evidence.title: Emergency report through the tracking ship.
evidence.body: The crew report an uncontrolled tumble after undocking. The report reaches the ground through Coastal Sentry Quebec.

provenance.note: Crisis receipt only; H1.

evidence.title: Crew regain control.
evidence.body: The crew have used the reentry control system to stabilize the spacecraft. The remaining mission objectives must be relinquished.

provenance.note: Later stabilization receipt; H2.

evidence.title: Return opportunities
evidence.body: Both opportunities return the crew to the western Pacific. An earlier landing gets them off the damaged spacecraft sooner, but the ship is hours away. Another orbit brings them down closer to the recovery force, with less RCS propellant left for entry.

provenance.note: Automatic at return planning; F7 simulated planning report. Western Pacific historical context only is H2.

evidence.title: Aircraft and recovery ship positions
evidence.body: Aircraft can support either return. At the earlier landing point, the nearest ship is hours away. At the later point, the recovery force can reach the capsule sooner.

provenance.note: Automatic at return planning; F4/F7. No real coordinates or ships assigned.

evidence.title: RCS propellant remaining
evidence.body: The spacecraft is stable for now. The reentry control system, or RCS, uses small thrusters to control its attitude during entry. Propellant is limited; using more before entry leaves less for that task. Mara is checking the remaining supply.

provenance.note: Automatic at return planning; F7. This is not actual Gemini VIII telemetry.

evidence.title: Pickup instruction confirmed
evidence.body: Elias and the DoD coordinator have agreed who sends the final pickup instruction to the ship. The readback is complete. This should prevent confusion during the approach, but the ship still has to reach the capsule.

provenance.note: Automatic at planning only if recovery preparation selected; F2/F7.

evidence.title: Warning call checked
evidence.body: Mara has checked the call with FLIGHT and CAPCOM. Both desks know to expect the RCS warning and her recommendation together, so CAPCOM can pass the instruction without waiting for the assessment to be repeated.

provenance.note: Automatic at planning only if systems preparation selected; F3/F7.

evidence.title: Instruction receipt checked
evidence.body: CAPCOM has identified who sends the next instruction and who confirms its receipt. Until that confirmation comes back, FLIGHT will treat the instruction as pending. The same check applies to either return.

provenance.note: Automatic at planning only if contact preparation selected; F1/F7.

evidence.title: Both crew members aboard the recovery ship.
evidence.body: Armstrong and Scott have been recovered alive. Their condition and the course of this return are recorded below.

provenance.note: Only at actual modeled pickup event. Alive recovery has H3 context; branch details F7.

evidence.title: Disagreement after Gemini VIII
evidence.body: Post-flight analysis has cleared Armstrong and Scott of blame. Walt Cunningham has criticized aspects of their performance; Tom Stafford has argued that undocking from Agena was the wrong decision. Gene Kranz has identified a failure on the ground: too few contingency procedures for the docked phase. Frank Borman and Wally Schirra have defended the crew.

provenance.note: Automatic only in the later post-flight scene. Attributed paraphrase of H5, a secondary account; not a transcript or an investigation document reproduced here.

constraint.text: The crew paid for the earlier return with a long sea wait. Recovery rehearsal is required. Choose the other exercise.
The extra orbit left the crew facing entry with critically low RCS propellant. A systems-warning drill is required. Choose the other exercise.

status_blocks.title: Astronaut corps divided
status_blocks.text: Your endorsement of the crew criticism still divides the corps. Armstrong and Scott enter future work with damaged confidence in you; Cunningham and Stafford's support is stronger.

status_blocks.title: Ground contingency work commissioned
status_blocks.text: The crew's confidence in you has strengthened. The critics haven't withdrawn their objections; work on docked-flight contingency procedures is under way.

mission-gemini-8.start_notice: A historical mission with fictional return decisions and alternate outcomes.

nodes.title: Mission briefing
nodes.text: Armstrong and Scott will rendezvous and dock with Agena. Before launch, you have time for two extra ground rehearsals: short practice runs on the communications loops, with controllers passing a report or instruction and checking that the right desk received it. The crew's training and mission rules are already in place; these exercises prepare the people in your room to work together under pressure.

nodes.prompt: Choose up to two supplemental ground rehearsals.
nodes.text: In the contact drill, Houston CAPCOM and a tracking-ship CAPCOM practice sending an instruction, reading it back, and confirming receipt to FLIGHT. In the recovery drill, Elias and the Department of Defense recovery coordinator practice passing the aircraft's location report to the ship and confirming who sends the pickup instruction. In the systems drill, Mara calls a low-propellant warning to FLIGHT and CAPCOM together, then passes her recommended response before the next entry task begins.

options.intent: Rehearse sending an instruction and confirming its receipt.
options.cost: Uses one of your two rehearsal opportunities.
options.uncertainty: A missed pass can still leave the instruction waiting for radio contact.
options.attraction: CAPCOM and the tracking station practice the readback before a time-critical call.

options.intent: Rehearse passing the pickup instruction from the recovery desk to the ship.
options.cost: Uses one of your two rehearsal opportunities.
options.uncertainty: The crew may still face a long wait if the nearest ship is far away.
options.attraction: Elias and the DoD coordinator settle who sends the pickup call before the recovery begins.

options.intent: Rehearse calling a low RCS propellant warning to FLIGHT and CAPCOM.
options.cost: Uses one of your two rehearsal opportunities.
options.uncertainty: The warning may arrive before Mara knows what caused it.
options.attraction: Mara practices getting her warning and recommended response to both desks promptly.

lines.speaker: g8-capcom
lines.text: Flight, Rose Knot Victor relays Armstrong's report: they're docked.

provenance.note: Crew report relayed through Houston; not a verbatim Lovell utterance. Original C is command pilot Armstrong.

nodes.title: Loss of contact
nodes.text: The scheduled tracking pass has ended. There's no new report from the spacecraft.

nodes.title: We'll have to wait for contact.

lines.speaker: g8-capcom
lines.text: Flight, we've lost the signal. We'll call at the next station.

provenance.note: Original procedural loss-of-signal/next-contact call for the game loop. Not a historical quotation.

lines.text: CAPCOM has left the next report's receipt blank. Nothing new has come through.

answer.speaker: g8-capcom
answer.text: The last report confirms docking. We've no new report on their attitude.

provenance.note: Docking confirmation paraphrased; absence of a current report is the procedural limit of this game contact gap.

lines.speaker: g8-capcom
lines.text: Flight, Coastal Sentry Quebec relays Scott: “We have serious problems here. We’re … tumbling end over end up here.” They’re disengaged from the Agena.

provenance.note: P identifies pilot Scott, not Armstrong. Quoted clauses retain the scan wording; ellipsis replaces the repeated “we’re”; apostrophe typography normalized. Final sentence paraphrases the same call. Houston relay framing is dramatized, not a recorded Lovell quote.

answer.speaker: g8-capcom
answer.text: CSQ's next report: Scott says they're slowly regaining control in RCS DIRECT. Armstrong says they're pulsing the RCS to reduce the roll.

provenance.note: Two successive crew updates closely paraphrased through the station; the optional question advances the report within the compressed crisis scene. No diagnosis or emotion inferred.

lines.speaker: g8-systems
lines.text: They've regained control using the reentry thrusters. They've used substantial propellant from both RCS rings. That means we terminate the mission.

lines.speaker: g8-systems
lines.text: Mara gives FLIGHT and CAPCOM the warning together, as rehearsed. The cause of the failure still isn't confirmed.

nodes.title: The rule
nodes.prompt: Terminate the mission after RCS use.

options.intent: Terminate the remaining mission and prepare the contingency return.
options.cost: The remaining docking work and EVA are canceled.
options.uncertainty: The room still needs to confirm the return plan and recovery support.
options.unavailable_reason: Requires the termination rule and the stabilization report.
options.attraction: Bring the crew home under the mission's contingency rules.

nodes.hint: Read the flight rule and the crew's stabilization report before confirming the return order.

nodes.title: Return planning
nodes.prompt: Bring them down now and leave them waiting at sea, or keep them in orbit with less propellant for entry?

lines.speaker: g8-flight-dynamics
lines.text: Two return opportunities. The first gets them down sooner. The second puts the recovery force closer. We can't have both.

lines.speaker: g8-systems
lines.text: Their condition is stable, for now. It might not be after another orbit.

lines.speaker: g8-recovery
lines.text: Every extra minute on the open ocean brings more risk to the crew. Take the later opportunity and the recovery force will be closer.

questions.text: What are the risks of an earlier return?

answer.speaker: g8-recovery
answer.text: The nearest ship is hours away. They'll be waiting in the capsule, in darkness, with the sea wearing them down. Air support helps, but it doesn't make the ship any closer.

questions.text: What are the risks of another orbit?

answer.speaker: g8-systems
answer.text: They'll spend another orbit in a damaged spacecraft. RCS propellant is already low; they need it to control their attitude during entry. If the warning or our instruction arrives late, they'll have less time to act.

questions.text: What's the crew saying, and how are they?

answer.speaker: g8-capcom
answer.text: Hawaii relays that Armstrong has the spacecraft under control, drifting slowly with limited control. We've no crew request choosing between these two return opportunities.

provenance.note: Control report from C at 07:39:53. The local discussion of areas 6-3/7-3 is ground-originated; it supplies no crew preference. The transcript records Flight preferring 7-3 at 07:39:39; that remains source history, not Lovell’s recommendation. Absence wording is bounded to the relayed reports at this decision, not a claim about every utterance in the mission.

options.intent: Bring them down at the earlier opportunity.
options.attraction: Mara backs ending their time aboard the damaged spacecraft sooner.
options.cost: The nearest ship is hours away. The crew will wait in the capsule at sea, in darkness, growing exhausted before pickup.
options.uncertainty: Confusion over the pickup call could leave them waiting even longer.
options.unavailable_reason: The contingency return has not been directed.

options.intent: Take the later opportunity after one more orbit.
options.attraction: Elias backs landing closer to the recovery force for a quicker pickup.
options.cost: The crew stay aboard as their RCS propellant becomes critically low. Mara must get the warning and entry recommendation through promptly.
options.uncertainty: A delayed warning or repeated instruction could force the crew to rush the entry preparations.
options.unavailable_reason: The contingency return has not been directed.

effects.label: Ordered the later return after one more orbit

nodes.hint: Ask Glen's questions and read each card's risks before choosing a return opportunity.

lines.speaker: g8-capcom
lines.text: Flight, splashdown report received. Both crew members responding.

provenance.note: Procedural receipt of the fictional earlier-route recovery report already established by this event; not a historical crew quotation or medical assessment.

lines.speaker: g8-recovery
lines.text: They're down. We still have to get the ship to them.

lines.speaker: g8-systems
lines.text: Flight, RCS propellant is critically low. They still need those thrusters for entry.

resolutions.text: The desks first settled who would send the pickup instruction, then called again to confirm receipt. That delayed the team's approach. By the time help reaches the capsule, both crew members are badly exhausted and need assistance getting aboard.
One call needed clarification or a repeat before the pickup team could proceed. The delay added to the crew's long wait at sea. Both are exhausted, but the team brings them aboard.

The pickup instruction reached the right desk and its receipt was confirmed on the first call. The team approaches without an additional delay. The sea wait has still worn the crew down; both are brought aboard.

Mara repeated the warning, and CAPCOM had to ask again for confirmation of the entry instruction. The delays left the crew rushing their final preparations with little RCS propellant remaining. They complete entry and reach the nearby recovery force visibly spent.

effects.label: Entry preparations rushed after two repeated calls

resolutions.text: One call had to be repeated before the room could confirm the entry instruction had been received. The crew completed their preparations under pressure, with little RCS propellant left. They reach the nearby recovery force tired but responsive.

effects.label: Entry preparations delayed by a repeated call

resolutions.text: Mara's warning reached FLIGHT and CAPCOM together, and the entry instruction was confirmed on the first call. RCS propellant remained critically low through entry. The crew reach the nearby recovery force tired but responsive.

nodes.title: Standing procedure

options.intent: Make every report say what's been confirmed and what's still unknown.
options.cost: You can make only one procedure the standing requirement.
options.uncertainty: The next tracking pass may still leave important questions unanswered.
options.unavailable_reason: Requires the recovered crew and the recorded relationship response.
options.attraction: Give the room a clear record of what was known and when.

options.intent: Put aircraft support, ship arrival, and confirmation of each on one recovery sheet.
options.cost: You can make only one procedure the standing requirement.
options.uncertainty: A correctly recorded request may still reach a ship too far away to help quickly.
options.unavailable_reason: Requires the recovered crew and the recorded relationship response.

nodes.hint: Read what each procedure changes, then choose the one you want to carry into the next mission.

nodes.title: Who carries the blame?
nodes.text: They came home. Now the argument moves from the flight room to the astronaut office. Some call the crew's judgment into question. Others ask what the ground failed to prepare for. Your position will tell the crews whether this room stands behind them when the checklist runs out.

nodes.title: Who carries the blame?

options.intent: Side with Cunningham and Stafford and blame the crew's handling of the emergency.
options.statement: I agree with the criticism. Armstrong and Scott's handling of the emergency deserves the blame.
options.attraction: Gain Cunningham and Stafford's support by backing their criticism.
options.cost: Armstrong and Scott lose trust in Glen, and division within the astronaut corps deepens.
options.uncertainty: The analysis has cleared the crew; your endorsement may prolong the argument rather than settle it.
options.unavailable_reason: Requires the recovered crew, the recorded relationship response, one baseline lesson, the post-flight context, and no prior stance.

effects.label: Glen sided with the crew's critics

options.intent: Accept responsibility for the ground's lack of docked-flight contingency procedures.
options.subtitle: Ground contingency procedures
options.statement: The ground didn't have enough contingency procedures for the docked phase. That's our failure, and we'll correct it. I won't blame Armstrong and Scott for bringing the spacecraft home.
options.attraction: Back the crew and commission procedures for emergencies while docked.
options.cost: Glen publicly accepts responsibility for a failure in the ground organization.
options.uncertainty: Cunningham and Stafford may keep their objections even after the ground begins corrective work.
options.unavailable_reason: Requires the recovered crew, the recorded relationship response, one baseline lesson, the post-flight context, and no prior stance.

outcomes.title: Crew recovered — earlier return, punishing sea wait
outcomes.result_line: Both crew members are back aboard, badly exhausted after the sea wait. Delays in the pickup calls made an already hard recovery worse.

outcomes.title: Crew recovered — earlier return, difficult pickup
outcomes.result_line: Both crew members are back aboard after a difficult pickup. A call that needed clarification or repeating added to their exhaustion.

outcomes.title: Crew recovered — earlier return, coordinated pickup
outcomes.result_line: The mission ended early, but the pickup was coordinated without an additional delay. Both crew members are aboard, worn down by the wait at sea.

outcomes.title: Crew recovered — extra orbit, rushed entry
outcomes.result_line: Both crew members are back after rushed entry preparations with little RCS propellant remaining. Repeated calls squeezed the time they had to get ready.

outcomes.title: Crew recovered — extra orbit, difficult entry preparations
outcomes.result_line: Both crew members are back after difficult entry preparations. A delayed warning or repeated instruction made the return harder.

outcomes.title: Crew recovered — extra orbit, prompt warning response
outcomes.result_line: The mission ended early, but the warning and entry instruction reached the crew promptly. Both crew members are back after an orderly response with little RCS propellant remaining.

debrief.text: Docking was achieved. The remaining objectives were terminated. Both crew members were recovered alive.
You chose to end spacecraft exposure sooner and accepted a prolonged sea recovery.
You chose another orbit to land closer to the recovery force. The crew completed entry with critically low RCS propellant.
The recovery drill established who would send the pickup instruction. The desks didn't need to settle that during pickup; the ship still had to cover the same distance.
The systems drill helped Mara get her warning to FLIGHT and CAPCOM together. She didn't have to repeat the assessment; the crew still had little RCS propellant left.
The contact drill helped CAPCOM confirm receipt on the first call. The room didn't need to ask again during the return.
Calls that needed clarification or repeating delayed the pickup or squeezed the crew's entry preparations. The crew-condition report records the result.
Elias's response is recorded above. The next mission must include a recovery rehearsal; you'll choose its companion exercise.
Mara's response is recorded above. The next mission must include a systems-warning rehearsal; you'll choose its companion exercise.
You added report timing and confirmation to the procedures binder.
You carried recovery cross-checking into the procedures binder.
You endorsed the criticism of Armstrong and Scott. Cunningham and Stafford's support grew, both crew members lost trust in you, and the astronaut corps became more divided.
You accepted responsibility for the missing ground procedures. The crew's trust in you grew, and you commissioned docked-flight contingency work.

Return timing — Historically, Gemini VIII landed in the western Pacific during its seventh revolution and the crew awaited USS Leonard F. Mason. You chose the game's earlier return. The particular ship delay, darkness, crew exhaustion, and rehearsal-dependent pickup sequence are alternate events, not a reconstruction of that recovery.

provenance.note: H6, p. 6-9: western Pacific zone 3 was available on revolutions 6 and 7; revolution 7 (the later opportunity) was selected. Timing attribution only; the game tradeoff and recovery consequences are dramatized. Original prose, not a quotation.

debrief.text: Return timing — You took the later opportunity, as history did: Gemini VIII landed in the western Pacific on its seventh revolution and the crew awaited USS Leonard F. Mason. The propellant warning, the closer pickup, and the crew-condition sequence on this route are dramatized, not a reconstruction of that recovery.

provenance.note: H6, p. 6-9: western Pacific zone 3 was available on revolutions 6 and 7; revolution 7 (the later opportunity) was selected. Timing attribution only; the game tradeoff and recovery consequences are dramatized. Original prose, not a quotation.

debrief.text: Accountability — Post-flight analysis cleared Armstrong and Scott, while Cunningham and Stafford criticized their handling of the emergency. Kranz instead faulted the ground's lack of docked-flight contingency procedures. You backed the crew's critics. Glen's statement, the increased division, and the changes in astronaut trust are alternate consequences of your choice.

provenance.note: Historical baseline and player-dependent interpretation; original prose, not a quotation.

debrief.text: Accountability — Kranz criticized the ground's lack of contingency procedures for docked flight; post-flight analysis cleared Armstrong and Scott. You took the same broad position on responsibility. Glen's words, the commissioned task, and the resulting trust changes are invented, and this choice doesn't return the rest of your campaign to the historical record.

provenance.note: Historical baseline and player-dependent interpretation; original prose, not a quotation.

plates.title: LEARNING TO FLY TOGETHER
plates.caption: Gemini's two-person missions are teaching NASA how to work in orbit: stay longer, meet another spacecraft, and dock. Those are skills Apollo will need for the journey to the Moon.

plates.title: THE CREW
plates.caption: Command pilot Neil Armstrong and pilot David Scott are flying Gemini VIII. Their mission calls for docking with an Agena target vehicle and a spacewalk by Scott.

plates.title: 16 MARCH 1966
plates.caption: The Agena launches first. A Titan II then lifts Armstrong and Scott from Cape Kennedy, beginning the chase toward their target in orbit.

plates.title: RENDEZVOUS AND DOCKING
plates.caption: Gemini VIII reaches the Agena, and Armstrong brings the two vehicles together. It's the first docking of two spacecraft in Earth orbit.

plates.title: BEYOND THE NEXT CONTACT
plates.caption: The spacecraft are joined, but Houston won't have continuous radio contact. The room will have to separate its last confirmed report from whatever happens beyond the next station's reach.

prologue.history_note: The Manned Spacecraft Center was renamed the Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center in 1973.
prologue.interpretation: The prologue is an illustrated mission overview, then an explicit return to earlier mission preparation. Staging, lighting and motion are artistic interpretations; the inflection caption is original scene-setting prose, not a transcript.

tiers.meaning: Crew recovered with the best available coordination in this scenario; the mission still ended early.
Crew recovered, with a significant difficulty during return or pickup.
Crew recovered, but severe exhaustion or compressed entry preparation made the recovery especially costly.
Reserved for future scenarios: a failed objective or recovery without necessarily losing a crew.

procedures.title: Report timing and confirmation
procedures.text: Record who sent each report, when the observation was made, and when it was received. List missing information separately and keep it unconfirmed until a new report arrives.

procedures.title: Recovery cross-check
procedures.text: List air support and surface retrieval separately; distinguish requested from confirmed support.

provenance.note: Original standing-procedure choice (F6). Adoption does not reverse the experienced outcome, trust, or compulsory rehearsal.

procedures.title: Docked-flight contingency development
procedures.text: Develop and rehearse procedures for emergencies while docked. List the symptoms the crew and ground can observe, agree who passes each warning, and prepare for a loss of contact before a diagnosis is complete.

provenance.note: A commissioned program task, not a completed engineering procedure, flight rule or proven safety improvement. Its wording and adoption are original F10, inspired by the reported Kranz criticism; not an exact historical NASA corrective document.

labels.start_notice: A historical mission with fictional return decisions and alternate outcomes.
labels.alternate_history_explanation: The earlier return order begins the alternate-history route. The later order follows the historical timing: the original mission report (H6, p. 6-9) records western Pacific zone 3 as available on revolutions 6 and 7, with revolution 7 selected. On either route, the game's propellant warning, recovery tradeoff, crew-condition sequence, controllers' reactions, and next-mission constraints are dramatized; matching the timing does not make these consequences a reconstruction of the recovery. The post-flight stance and its relationship consequences are fictional. The historical opening — docking, the communications gap, the crew's stabilization of the spacecraft, the termination rule, and a western Pacific recovery — follows sources H1–H4. Once the earlier order activates ALTERNATE HISTORY, a later historical choice does not reset it.
labels.capcom_history_note: Houston CAPCOM for Gemini VIII was Jim Lovell. His calls in the game are dramatized from the mission's air-ground transcript (H7); the crew's quoted words are from that transcript.

fiction.title: Contact rehearsal
fiction.text: Supplemental sender/acknowledgement exercise, readback document and its later ground handoff effects. These are performed fictional rehearsals, not astronaut training prerequisites.

fiction.title: Recovery rehearsal
fiction.text: Supplemental pickup ownership/readback exercise and the fictional rework it can avoid. Preparation does not move recovery forces closer.

fiction.title: Systems rehearsal
fiction.text: Supplemental warning-routing exercise, its readback and its operational handoff effects. Preparation does not add control reserve or identify the hardware fault.

fiction.title: Air-support and surface-retrieval reports
fiction.text: Original abstract status reports, now supporting a real operational choice. No claim to historical ship/aircraft positions.

fiction.title: Recovery coordination events
fiction.text: The fictional ground ownership clarification, acknowledgement retry and pickup approach consequences. These are explicitly events of the game room, not errors by historical astronauts or operators.

fiction.title: Procedure adoption
fiction.text: Two original standing-procedure choices and their reference pages. Neither reverses the operational outcome or the next-mission rehearsal constraint.

fiction.title: Alternate return envelope and outcomes
fiction.text: Both selectable opportunities, extra modeled orbit, ordinal critical-reserve warning, earlier sea wait, concentrated later pickup, all six execution/consequence cases, all crew-condition variations, and the six outcome titles. Both routes are authored to be viable in this simplified scenario and both end with the crew alive. There are no numerical chances or hidden survival roll. Actual orbital feasibility, exact fuel quantities, precise recovery time and medical diagnoses are not asserted. Neither branch is labeled the exact historical result. All figures who execute onboard operations remain competent. H6 confirms a historical choice of return revolution; the fictional element is this menu’s specific operational tradeoff and outcomes, not the existence of a timing decision.

fiction.title: Named fictional controllers and operational relationships
fiction.text: Mara Voss and Elias Reed, their recommendations, recovery responses, trust-point changes and notes. These are original characters reusing the SYSTEMS and RECOVERY portrait slots. Negative trust never suppresses safety information. The separate user-authorized astronaut relationship branch is F10.

fiction.title: Gemini IX-A planning constraints
fiction.text: Compulsory recovery or systems rehearsal following the experienced return risk; the three offered two-exercise plans; branch eligibility; and the player's persisted plan commitment. These are operational preparation consequences in the fictional campaign, not the historical IX-A roster, schedule or training program.

fiction.title: Post-flight stance and social consequences
fiction.text: Glen's two statements; the compressed later discussion scene; blaming the crew versus accepting ground contingency responsibility; Armstrong/Scott trust -2 each and Cunningham/Stafford +1 each plus a deepened corps rift on the blame route; Armstrong/Scott +1 each and critics unchanged on the ground route; all associated narration, facts, notes and IX-A relationship displays; and the concrete commissioned docked-contingency task. These are fictional consequences of the player's choice. The ground-side criticism itself is sourced through H5, but its exact implementation and resulting relationship gains are not asserted as historical events. Choosing to blame the crew does not change their demonstrated actions or the source's reported exoneration. Choosing ground responsibility does not erase the existence of disagreement.

fiction.title: Illustrated prologue and recovery presentation
fiction.text: Original staged illustrations, lighting, weather, visual motion, the overview-to-preparation transition, recovery tier labels and result-line summaries. The six underlying game outcomes remain the simplified model described in F7. Different plate lighting expresses tone, not a measured recovery time, storm, medical finding or new consequence. Portrait expressions represent the game relationship changes in F8 and F10; they do not document the real astronauts’ feelings or add their words.

Failure is Not an Option — home
FAILURE IS NOT AN OPTION A FLIGHT DIRECTOR GAME
Two astronauts. A damaged spacecraft. The next call is yours.
Gemini VIII · Play in your browser
History sets the scene. Your decisions shape what follows.
Take the flight director’s seat in a narrative game inspired by real missions and the people who made them possible.

You are Glen Kurtz: a fictional tribute to the legendary Gene Kranz, whose leadership helped guide Mission Control through pivotal moments of Gemini and Apollo. The signature vest is a nod to Kranz; Glen’s story is his own. Ageless by design, he represents generations of flight directors, from the earliest missions to those still ahead.

Listen to your controllers. Weigh incomplete information. Make the call, then live with its consequences. Follow the historical path or branch into an alternate outcome. The astronauts are real; the decisions and consequences blend documented events with clearly identified fiction.
Your controllers see different risks. Ask questions and work through the evidence before you commit.
Getting the crew home means weighing time in orbit against the conditions awaiting them at sea.
Your preparations and orders affect the return. Your response afterward shapes relationships and the next planning step.
GEMINI VIII The Weight of the Call
A historic docking. A sudden emergency. Armstrong and Scott have brought their spacecraft back under control. Now your team must bring them home.
Prepare your controllers, weigh competing return risks, and face the consequences of your decision in the post-flight discussion.

A lifelong dream. A new trajectory.
I’m Dan Lee-Odinson, a Technical Project Manager and Space Studies student at Everglades University.

My fascination with space began when I was six, holding my breath as Discovery’s STS-26 crew launched on the historic Return to Flight after the Challenger disaster. Watching Artemis II lift off in April 2026 turned that lifelong passion into a determination to be part of what comes next.
Since then, I’ve been working toward one goal: to learn everything I can and bring my skills to a future career in Mission Operations and Program Management.

I’m inspired by the people of NASA and the space agencies and companies around the world expanding what humanity can do in space—and by the dedication of everyone on the ground who makes those journeys possible.
This game is my tribute to you all.
